abstract.para: &rear; (&rear.long;) is a disaster recovery framework designed to help system administrators re-create Linux infrastructure after a system failure. It is a collection of Bash scripts that need to be adjusted to the specific production environment that is to be protected in case of disaster.

By generating a system-specific bootable rescue image paired with automated file restoration workflows, &rear; enables rapid bare-metal recovery and disk layout reconstruction on identical target hardware.
complements file backup software by handling the low-level system and disk layout recreation required for bare-metal disaster recovery

section.title: What is disaster recovery?
section.para: A system in a production environment might be destroyed unexpectedly because of broken hardware, misconfiguration or software problems. Disaster recovery means re-creating the system, either on the same hardware or on identical replacement hardware. Re-creating a system involves not just restoring the system's files from a backup, but also preparing the system's disk layout (such as partitioning, file systems and mount points) and reinstalling the boot loader.
No disaster recovery solution works out-of-the-box. Therefore, you must prepare for a disaster before it happens.

section.title: What is a disaster recovery plan?
section.para: Before a disaster happens, create a disaster recovery plan so that any system administrator knows exactly what to do and has a complete procedure to follow when the disaster happens.

listitem.para: Conduct a risk analysis of your infrastructure. List all the possible threats and evaluate how serious they are. Determine how likely these threats are and what their impact would be.
The outcome of the analysis is an overview of which risks can be tolerated and which would be critical. Determine how you can minimize these risks and how much it costs to do so.
Make checklists, test procedures, establish and assign priorities, and inventory your IT infrastructure. Define how to deal with problem if any services in your infrastructure fail.
After defining a plan, test it thoroughly and regularly on hardware that is identical to your main IT infrastructure.

section.title: How does disaster recovery with &rear; work?
section.para: &rear; uses Bash scripts to analyze a running system and create a disaster recovery system, which includes a recovery installer and either an integrated or external file backup. You must configure &rear; for your specific system and infrastructure, including what to back up, how to create and store the recovery system, and what the recovery installer does.
For the file backup, &rear; can use internal backup tools like tar or work with third-party backup tools like EMC NetWorker. For a full list of supported file backup options, run man rear.

If the system is destroyed, you can boot the recovery installer from a physical medium or over the network. The recovery installer re-creates the system by preparing the disk layout (such as partitioning, file systems and mount points), restoring the files from the backup, and reinstalling the boot loader.

section.title: Can I update &rear;?
section.para: Version updates for &rear; are provided as separate packages that intentionally conflict with each other to prevent your installed version getting accidentally replaced with another version. If you have a tested and fully functional disaster recovery procedure with one &rear; version, do not update &rear;. Keep the &rear; package and do not change your disaster recovery method.
In the following cases you need to re-validate your existing disaster recovery procedure:

listitem.para: When you update any software that is used by &rear;.
If you update low-level system components such as parted, btrfs and similar.
